submission.natural_language_explanation: L9/N613+ fires on a token that lies inside a repeat of a multi-token span that already appeared earlier in the same context: it tracks the model's copy/repeat (induction) signal, not the token's identity, peaking a few tokens into the second or later copy of a repeated URL/version string, import path, IP address, timestamp, table row, error or boilerplate line, or repeated sentence. The first occurrence of the same material, a paraphrase of it, and any non-repeated text stay at the token's own baseline (usually 0-0.5, at most ~1.5 for IP-like digit strings), while each additional copy raises the peak (a repeated import line: 0.06 at one copy, 1.73 at two, 2.90 at three, ~3.05 at four or more, saturating) at almost any copy-to-copy distance (0-80 tokens tested); plain narrative prose repeated only twice sits at the weak end of the same scale (0.3-0.5), so the copy signal is graded by how distinctive the repeated string is.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
Lighthouses on the northern coast were, for most of the nineteenth century, maintained by a small corps of keepers who lived on site with their families. Records from the period describe a routine that changed little from one station to the next. Keepers trimmed wicks, polished lenses, and logged the hours of darkness in bound ledgers that were inspected twice a year by a district inspector. The ledgers themselves have survived in surprising numbers, and historians now use them to reconstruct weather patterns, shipping traffic, and the slow arrival of new technology.

The transition to acetylene and later to electric lamps disrupted this routine. A keeper who had spent decades tending an oil lamp suddenly had to learn about mantles, regulators, and eventually generators. Training was uneven. Some districts sent instructors from station to station; others simply mailed a manual and expected the keeper to work it out alone. Complaints about the manual's clarity fill the correspondence of the 1890s, and the same phrases appear in letters from stations hundreds of miles apart, suggesting that the wording was copied from a single circular.

Automation arrived in stages. First came clockwork mechanisms that wound the lamp and rotated the lens without an attendant. Then came remote monitoring, which allowed a district office to see whether a light was burning without sending anyone to the rock. By the middle of the twentieth century, most stations on the northern coast had been converted to unattended operation, and the keepers' cottages were either demolished or sold to private owners.

The archive that documents all this was nearly lost. In 1978 a warehouse fire destroyed roughly a third of the district records, and the surviving ledgers were moved to a university library where they sat uncatalogued for almost twenty years. A volunteer group began sorting them in the late 1990s. Their finding aid, first posted at https://archive.example.edu/lighthouse/ledgers, listed every surviving volume by station and year. The same page was later revised to include photographs, and a note explains that the address has been kept stable so that citations in older papers still resolve.

Researchers who use the collection often begin with the annual summaries, which compress a year of nightly entries into a few lines of totals. The summaries are less vivid than the daily logs but far easier to search. A typical summary records the number of nights lit, the gallons of oil consumed, the hours of fog signal operation, and any unusual events such as wrecks, rescues, or equipment failures.

Digitising the ledgers created its own problems. The bindings had to be cut, the pages photographed under controlled light, and the resulting images checked against the originals. Volunteers transcribed a portion of the text, enough to make the whole set searchable but far short of a complete transcription. The catalogue page at https://archive.example.edu/lighthouse/ledgers now links to both the page images and the partial transcriptions, and it warns that the two do not always agree.

The first occurrence of the same material, a paraphrase of it, and any non-repeated text stay at the token's own baseline (usually 0-0.5, at most ~1.5 for IP-like digit strings), while each additional copy raises the peak (a repeated import line: 0.06 at one copy, 1.73 at two, 2.90 at three, ~3.05 at four or more, saturating) at almost any copy-to-copy distance (0-80 tokens tested); plain narrative prose repeated only twice sits at the weak end of the same scale (0.3-0.5), so the copy signal is graded by how distinctive the repeated string is.
